body.p: Claims 1-15 are pending in the application. Applicant amends claims 1, 5 and 15, cancels claims 3, 4, 8, 13 and 14, and adds new claims 16-25. No new matter has been added by this amendment. Applicant respectfully traverses the rejections; however, Applicant amends the application to further prosecution and requests reconsideration.
body.h1: Claim Rejections Under 35 U.S. C. Q 112(b)
body.p: Claims 3-12 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 112(b), as being indefinite.

The Office Action rejects claims 3-6, 8, and 11-12 for the term "wing-like" being a relative term which renders the claim indefinite. Applicant amends the claims to require a "wing body" or a "wing aerodynamic profile".
The Office Action rejects claims 11-12 for the term " airfoil-like " being a relative term which renders the claim indefinite. Applicant amends the claims to require a "airfoil extension".
Applicant submits that the claims are now defined with the relative term removed, and in view of the specification and drawings, and respectfully requests withdrawal of the objection.
body.h1: Claim Rejections Under 35 U.S. C. Q 102
body.p: Claims 1-8 and 14-15 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1) as being anticipated by U.S. Patent No. 2,473,329 to Candler.
Independent claim 1 is amended to include additional limitations, including limitations that were previously presented in dependent claims 3, 4, 8, 13 and 14.
Claim 13 was not rejected as being anticipated by Candler, and therefore Applicant submits that amended claim 1 and its dependent are patentable over the reference.
body.h1: Claim Rejections Under 35 U.S. C. Q 103

p.u: ection of claims 9-10 over Candler in view of Avery and Bordole

body.p: Claims 9-10 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Candler, in view of U.S. Patent No. 2,369,652 to Avery, and U.S. Publication No. 2016/0083083 to Bordoley.

Claims 9-10 depend from claim 1. Claim 1 is amended to include limitations from dependent claim 13. Claim 13 was not rejected as being obvious over Candler in view of Avery and Bordeloy, and therefore Applicant submits that amended claim 1 is patentable over the combination of references.

Applicant also submits that the Office Action relies on Bordeloy for coaxial mounting of a torsion spring on a vane, and that the reference does not teach or provide the limitation of amended claim 1, including the limitations associated with the stator blade.

Claims 11-12 depend from claim 1. Claim 1 is amended to include limitations from dependent claim 13. Claim 13 was not rejected as being obvious over Candler in view of Avery and Bordeloy, and therefore Applicant submits that amended claim 1 is patentable over the combination of references.

body.p: Claim 13 was rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being obvious over Candler, in view of Avery.
Claim 13 is cancelled, and limitations of claim 13 are added to claim 1. Amended independent claim 1 now requires:
a stator with a gearbox fairing mounted to the shroud for supporting the rotatable rotor hub in the transverse duct, wherein the stator comprises at least one rotatable

body; and

p.u: wherein the aerodynamic center is spaced apart from the rotation axis, and the rotation axis is arranged closer to the leading edge of than the aerodynamic center, in front of the aerodynamic center, thus producing an airflow induced pressure on the win
ue moment which provokes rotation of the wing body around the rotation axis into a position of reduced aerodynamic

body.p: (Emphasis added).

The Office Action indicates that Candler discloses a rotorcraft with stator blades 39, and relies on Avery to teach "a ducted tail rotor with rotatable stator blades Fig. 3: vanes 34 that rotate in response to an airflow induced pressure generated by an airflow acting on the at least one rotatable stator blade Col 4, lines 56-65".

The Office Action indicates that "It would have been obvious ... to have modified the invention disclosed by Nall Candler by having the at least one rotatable stator blade rotates in response to an airflow induced pressure generated by an airflow acting on the at least one rotatable stator blade as disclosed by Avery."

The Office Action further indicates that one skilled in the art "would have been motivated to make this modification to "normally hold all the slats yieldably in closed position with a force so proportioned that when propeller 211s brought into action the pressures created 80 by the propeller slip stream immediately rotate the slats on their respective pivots to align them with the airstream" (Avery, Col 4, lines 56-65)."

Applicant respectfully disagrees, and submits that the combination of references does not disclose, teach or suggest each and every limitation of claim 1, or in the alternative, teaches away from the limitations of claim 1.

Generally, Candler describes a helicopter that comprises a forward body portion 10 that terminates at its rear in an elongated trailing tail portion 11. In Candler, the tail portion 11 at its rear end 16 and has a funnel shaped transverse opening 17. A plurality of radially disposed blades

38 are rotatably mounted in the funnel shaped transverse opening 17 on a housing 21, and louver devices forming blades 39 are also arranged in the opening 17. Candler teaches that an operator controls the angular positions of louver devices forming blades 39 via manipulation of control levers or handles in the cabin that are connected to control cables and pulleys 40-41 and the blades 39 to control the position of the blades 39 to allow the operator to regulate the air entering the passageway. (See, for example, Column 4, lines 54-68, and Column 5, lines 35-40).

Thus, the operator of the helicopter controls the blades 39 to predetermined angles to regulate the direction and the quantity of the air delivered to the radially disposed rotating rotor blades 38. Candler teaches that "The improvements are especially applicable for opposing the torque developed in the fuselage of a helicopter, by an overhead propeller that rotates on a vertical axis. Also provision is made for controlling this air current by means of adjustable swinging louvers that have fixed axes and which do not rotate with the bladed impeller. This arrangement eliminates the size and weight, and materially simplifies the complicated mechanism usually employed for changing the pitch of the blades of a tail rotor." (Emphasis added, Column 1, lines 30-48). Candler further teaches that this is used for control in that "To increase or diminish and thus control the direction and quantity of air passing through the annular opening 11 the louvers or blades 39 may be tilted to different angles thus predetermining the amount of lateral pressure exerted by the air current against the ambient air." (Column 5, lines 50-56).

As discussed above, Candler requires that an operator control the position of the louver blades, and uses this control, at least in part, to simplify the mechanism for changing pitch of the tail rotor blades and to control the airflow through the tail rotor and the lateral pressure provided therefrom. In Candler, the louvers 39 are controlled manually thorough the action of a crew member, and one skilled in the art would not look to change an operator controlled position that is independent of airflow as taught by Candler to the claimed limitation with the position of the stator blade rotating based on airflow induced pressure to reduce the drag.
Applicant therefore submits that Candler teaches away from the limitations of claim 1 such that claim 1 and its dependents are nonobvious and patentable over the combination of Candler and Avery.

Furthermore, Applicant submits that Candler therefore does not teach, suggest, or provide any reason to have a stator blade that is mounted to gearbox fairing and the shroud such that "an airflow induced pressure on the wing aerodynamic profile generating a torque moment which provokes rotation of the wing body around the rotation axis into a position of reduced aerodynamic drag" as is required by claim 1,
Avery therefore does not teach, suggest, or provide any reason to have a stator blade that is mounted to gearbox fairing and the shroud such that an airflow induced pressure on the wing
aerodynamic profile generating a torque moment which provokes rotation of the wing body around the rotation axis into a position of reduced aerodynamic drag as is required by claim 1.

Therefore, since the combination of Candler and Avery does not teach, suggest, or provide a stator blade that is mounted to a gearbox fairing and shroud such that an airflow induced pressure on the wing aerodynamic profile generating a torque moment which provokes rotation of the wing body around the rotation axis into a position of reduced aerodynamic drag as is required by claim 1, claim 1 and its dependents are patentable over the combination of references.
New Claims
